findings.problem: decision_logic[6] ends with an unqualified instruction: if the s. 19D(a) limit applies and nothing indicates the s. 19D(b) exception, 'confirm with the prescriber before filling rather than rewriting the quantity'. drug_examples[1] likewise calls a longer first adult oxycodone prescription 'one to confirm with the prescriber before filling'. Elsewhere the section itself says the statute does not answer whether the pharmacist must inquire, and presents confirmation as the course that is safe on either reading (orientation[7], worked_examples[2].steps[4], retrieval_prompts[14]). Without that qualifier, these two summary items can be read as a legal duty to call the prescriber.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19D is addressed only to the practitioner ('a practitioner shall not issue'). It rests the exception on the practitioner's professional medical judgment and puts the triggering condition in the patient's medical record. 247 CMR 9.15(1) and (2) contain no requirement to contact the prescriber, and the Department's prescriber update describes the seven-day restriction only as a limit on what a prescriber may issue. The advice is lawful and prudent, matches the section's hedged analysis, and would not lead a candidate to a wrong or unlawful course on Massachusetts facts, so decision_logic still passes. Adding the qualifier used elsewhere (for example 'the safe course is to confirm ...') would close the gap in modality.

findings.problem: The third row of the table 'What a Massachusetts prescriber holds, by schedule' is labelled 'A schedule covered by one registration but not by the other' and concludes that the prescriber 'is not registered for that schedule in the way the page requires'. The row is not limited to Schedules II through V. Read literally, it would treat Schedule VI as a mismatch, even though a Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration covers Schedule VI and a DEA registration never does.
findings.rationale: The Department's registration page states the same-schedules requirement for activity with Schedules II through V. 105 CMR 700.004 registers physicians, dentists, podiatrists and veterinarians for Massachusetts Schedule VI and for the same schedules as their DEA registration. The rows immediately above, orientation[5], decision_logic[4] and ma_vs_federal[2] all state the Schedule VI rule correctly, so a candidate is unlikely to be misled. Relabelling the row as 'a schedule in II through V' would make the cell accurate on its own.

results.summary: Read every field against current official text. The section quotes or paraphrases faithfully: 21 CFR 1306.04(a) (eCFR, current to 9/10/2026); 247 CMR 9.15 (12/6/2024 publication); 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) and (A)(2) (2/2/2024 publication); the Version 5.2 Data Submission Guide for Dispensers; the DPH registration page, read with 105 CMR 700.004; and M.G.L. c. 94C, ss. 18B, 19(a) and 19D. On 21 CFR 1306.04(a), it attaches 'knowingly' to the penalty for filling a purported prescription, not to the pharmacist's corresponding responsibility. On 247 CMR 9.15, it lists exactly the four 9.15(2) determinations and the 9.15(1) duty to register with, and keep login information for, MassPAT. It adds no PMP query or registration check as a determination, and 105 CMR 700.012(G) places the PMP-utilization duty on prescribers. On reporting, it keeps the pharmacy's duty separate from the pharmacist's: Schedule II-V and additional-drug dispensing pursuant to a prescription is reported, out-of-state deliveries included, and hospital inpatient medication orders are excluded. On registration, it states the MCSR and DEA structure by schedule correctly. On s. 19D, it teaches the adult and minor triggers, the s. 19D(b) grounds with documentation in the medical record, and the s. 19D(c) exclusion. It correctly treats s. 19D as binding only the practitioner: quantity alone does not show a prescription invalid, and the pharmacist has no authority to shorten the supply. On s. 18B, it assigns the (c) knowledge standard to the outpatient pharmacist and the (e) reckless-or-negligent standard to licensed health care providers generally. As the section assumes, gabapentin is in none of 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15 and tramadol is in 1308.14. There are two Low findings. First, decision_logic[6] and drug_examples[1] drop the hedge that elsewhere presents prescriber confirmation as the safe course rather than a legal requirement. Second, one registration-table row is not confined to Schedules II-V. Neither would mislead a candidate on Massachusetts facts. Two verification notes, neither a defect. (1) 247 CMR 2.00 defines Practitioner by reference to M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, which defines practitioners by registration. The known-registration-gap analysis the section calls arguable therefore has more textual support than it says, and its conclusion (do not fill until resolved) is correct. (2) Pharmacists also report naloxone doses under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19B(d), which DPH now asks pharmacies to include in daily PMP submissions. This is outside the section's declared 700.012 scope, and the section does not contradict it. All 16 listed practice questions are answerable from the section, and neither the section nor any question's explanation contradicts the other.
